News.title: Laos gold hunters growing ‘hungry & weak’ after 9 days in 1,000ft-deep cave – as rescuers describe ‘diving into coffee’
News.content:
GOLD hunters trapped inside a flooded cave in Laos are growing “hungry and weak” following nine days of hell stuck in a 1,000ft-deep chamber.

Rescue workers also described plunging “into coffee” during the gruelling search operation – which also faces the terrifying prospect of collapsing walls.





The group of Lao nationals became trapped last week after venturing into the cave in Xaisomboun province in search of gold.

A landslide triggered by torrential rain blocked their exit and turned the cave into a watery prison.

Five of the seven have thankfully been found alive after more than a week underground – but two are still missing.

The survivors are believed to have been kept alive by a pocket of continuous airflow – a narrow lifeline in an otherwise suffocating labyrinth now filling with rising floodwater.



Australian expert rescue diver diver Josh Richards, who has now joined the search, said the biggest risk the search team faced was collapsing mud walls, while also highlighting the prospect of further flooding.

He told Australia’s ABC News: “It’s all clay, it’s all soft, it’s all mud.



“There’s not a lot holding the roof up. If you’ve seen the water that we’re heading into, you can’t see anything.

“It’s like diving into coffee.”

Laos authorities are rushing to pump water out of the cave system to ease the operation – but there is still a flooded section.



Richards said: “At this stage it sounds like there’s still a significant sump of water that we’ll need to try and get people out through in order to get them out of the cave.”

Laos is also facing its monsoon season – with storms at risk of quickly refilling the cavern.

Astonishing footage has also shown one of the survivors named Ee telling a rescue worker about how is chest is in pain and his throat is sore.



He says in the clip: “We’re weak and we’re really hungry.”

“Please bring rice and some proper food.”

Fellow expert diver Mikko Paasi said finding the group was an “overwhelming” and “emotional” moment.

The Thai-based Finnish diving specialist told Australia’s ABC News: “That was an emotional moment, like what are the chances?



“We believed they were still alive, but the odds were quite low given everything.”

“Ascending to the final chamber where they were and seeing them sitting there all grey and all pale but in good spirits.

“They were very happy, there were tears, big smiles from both sides.

“The feeling of not giving up, and succeeding… now we are one step closer to getting them back out to their families and kids. It was overwhelming.”



Paasi also said the cave passages are so narrow that divers taking part in the mission needed to be “slim” and “hard-headed”.

He added that his colleagues had to weigh less than 70kg to navigate through the tiny maze.

“If claustrophobia had a form, this would be it,” Paasi said.



He emphasises how rescue workers had to “wriggle through like a worm” to get to the chamber.

Rescue teams are still scrambling to secure more oxygen tanks as conditions inside the cave worsen by the hour.

Kengkard Bongkawong, head of operations for Thailand’s Metta Tham Rescue, has issued an urgent appeal for equipment.



“We need to borrow as many oxygen tanks as possible and want to set up an oxygen refilling station in front of the cave.”

It comes after footage showed the trapped gold hunters sending emotional messages to their families.

One man said: “Mum, my wife, my child, don’t worry about me. They’ve reached us already.”

Kham added: “Tomorrow or the day after, I should be able to get out. My wife, stay strong and wait for me.”

Another villager, Ing, said: “Don’t worry mum. The rescue team has reached us now. We’re safe. I miss mum and dad so much.”



Mued said: “Mum and dad, I’m still strong, I’ll be able to go home soon. Love you mum and dad.”

In another clip, Laen can be heard saying: “I’ll come out and see you soon.”

And the final member of the five discovered said simply: “Don’t worry. I’m still strong.”

Paasi previously warned the operation is far from straightforward, saying the extraction plan “ain’t going to be easy”.

Heavy rain and brutal mountain terrain are hampering every stage of the rescue, with teams working around the clock to pump out water and rig ropes through the cave’s deadly passages.



Some tunnels narrow to just 23 inches wide, forcing rescuers to crawl through razor-sharp rock while carrying life-saving equipment – all as oxygen levels continue to drop.

The mission has drawn comparisons to the 2018 Thai cave rescue, when 12 boys and their football coach were sedated and guided out through submerged tunnels.

But Richards said: “The cave is significantly smaller than the one that the soccer team was rescued from in Thailand, not just in length, but actually in physical size.”

He also told ABC that the cave the survivors are trapped in looked “scary as hell”, despite his wide-ranging experience.

Richards added: “I’m pretty scared, if I’m honest. The stuff that Mikko has shared via video should scare anybody who watches it.”



The cave lies in a remote, mountainous area of Xaisomboun province, around 75 miles north of the capital Vientiane, making access extremely difficult.

Rescuers have so far reached around 330 feet into the cave, with the remaining trapped men believed to be a further 100 feet inside – separated by a waterlogged maze of rock and darkness.

The escape route, a 1,115-foot tunnel requiring divers to squeeze through tight gaps and navigate near-zero visibility, remains one of the most dangerous parts of the operation.

After more than a week underground, fears are growing as time runs out and conditions inside continue to deteriorate.

News.title: Man, 21, dies after horror smash between e-scooter and fire engine ‘travelling to an emergency’
News.content:
CRASH TRAGEDY Man, 21, dies after horror smash between e-scooter and fire engine ‘travelling to an emergency’

A MAN has tragically died after a fire engine “travelling to a reported emergency” crashed into an e-scooter.

Emergency services rushed to a junction in Dartford, Kent at 10.44pm on Monday where the scooter rider, 21, was found injured.



He was rushed to a hospital in a serious condition but tragically died on Wednesday.

Police are appealing for witnesses or dashcam footage to come forward.



Ann Millington, Chief Executive at Kent Fire and Rescue Service (KFRS), said: “At approximately 10.40pm on May 25, a fire engine was involved in a collision with an electric scooter in Princes Road, Dartford.

“The fire engine was travelling to a reported emergency.

“Kent Police has confirmed the rider of the electric scooter has sadly died.

“Our deepest condolences and thoughts are with everyone affected by this incident.

“There is a legal process to follow, and we are fully committed to supporting Kent Police’s investigation, as well as conducting our own internal investigation.”

News.title: Man and woman plead not guilty to murdering ‘giggly & happy’ toddler who was rushed to hospital with horror injuries
News.content:
TOT TRAGEDY Man and woman plead not guilty to murdering ‘giggly & happy’ toddler who was rushed to hospital with horror injuries

A MAN and woman have pleaded not guilty to murdering a “giggly and happy” baby who died after being rushed to hospital with horror injuries.

Tobias-John Doyle was aged just 21 months when he was tragically passed away on December 2, 2023.





Omiel Gordon, 35, and Shalom Morgan, 23, appeared at Leicester Crown Court today where they pleaded not guilty to murder.

The pair also denied causing or allowing the death of a child and child cruelty.

A trial set to last eight weeks has been scheduled for January 25 next year.

Judge Timothy Spencer KC told Gordon and Morgan they would next have to appear in court in October.

He said: “You are both in a very serious position, I think you both know that.

“You will both stand trial for murder on Monday January 25.

“You will be back before me on October 23 when we will see how this case is shaping up.

“You will both be brought before me. Until then, you will both remain in custody. Go down.”



The pair were first arrested in November 2023 after Tobias was taken to hospital from home in Leicester.

Family liaison officers have been supporting the family throughout the probe.

Tobias’ dad Simon previously paid tribute, saying: “Tobias was my best friend.

“He was a giggly, happy little boy who put a smile on everyone’s face. He had the most beautiful chubby cheeks and curly hair and he absolutely loved dinosaurs.

“We love him and miss him so much.”

News.title: Midlands Air Festival 2026 schedule: Full list of aircraft and timetable of displays
News.content:
AVIATION fans are in for a treat as the Midlands Air Festival returns to Warwickshire’s historic Ragley Hall.

Here’s everything you need to know about this year’s stunning spectacle, headlined by the world-famous Red Arrows.





When is the Midlands Air Festival 2026?

The Midlands Air Festival is back at Ragley Hall for its eighth edition from Friday, May 29 to Sunday, May 31, 2026.

In 2025, over 30,000 people descended on the Alcester estate over the course of the three-day weekend.

The famous RAF Red Arrows are headlining a stacked line-up of WW2 warbirds, military jets, helicopters and hot air balloons.

There’s also the festival’s trademark Nightfire pyrotechnic and firework display to enjoy on the Friday night.



What aircraft are flying at the Midlands Air Festival 2026?

The line-up features classic aeroplanes rubbing shoulders with cutting-edge aerobatic teams, military jets and rare rotary aircraft.

The Red Arrows headline the bill with their new-season displays, joined by the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight – featuring the Dakota, Spitfire and Hurricane – and the RAF Falcons mass parachute team.

WW2 stars include the mighty four-engine B-17 Flying Fortress, the P-51 Mustang fighter, the Fairey Swordfish from the Navy Wings Heritage Flight, the Catalina seaplane and the Harvard trainer.

Vintage biplane buffs can enjoy the Stampe display team, while military fans will be treated to the Vietnam-era Bronco turboprop and the Strikemaster Jet Pair.



The imposing MiG-17 fighter jet is also slated to appear, subject to airworthiness certification.

Aerobatic highlights include the Extra 300S, the Sydney Charles Display Team, Team Raven and Supermarine Spitfire Mk IXB MH434.

Rounding out the line-up are the Grumman Turbo Firecat, SIAI-Marchetti SF260, Diamond DA42 Twinstar and Calidus Autogyro.

The Westland Sea King and Westland Whirlwind will also feature in two Historic Helicopters role demonstrations.

Friday’s Nightfire programme includes a model aircraft airfield attack display, followed by pyrotechnic air displays.



What is the Midlands Air Festival 2026 schedule?

12.30pm to 3pm: Hot Air Balloon Tethering

3pm to 3.30pm: Model Aircraft Display

3.30pm to 7pm: Air Display

7pm to 8.45pm: Hot Air Balloon Mass Ascent

8.55pm to 9.15pm: Model Aircraft Airfield Attack Display

9.20pm to 9.45pm: Nightfire — Pyro Air Displays

9.50pm to 10.30pm: Nightfire — Hot Air Balloon Night Glow

10.30pm to 10.35pm: Nightfire — Firework Finale

11.30pm: Gates close

5.30am: Car parks and event opens

6am to 8am: Hot Air Balloon Mass Ascent

9am to 10am: Model Aircraft Display

News.title: My son, 5, was abducted by his dad who was wrongly released from jail in shock blunder – I’ve no idea where they are
News.content:
‘MY LIFE IS OVER’ My son, 5, was abducted by his dad who was wrongly released from jail in shock blunder – I’ve no idea where they are

THE mother of a five-year-old who was abducted by his father says she feels “betrayed” by UK prison authorities who accidentally let him out of jail.

Claire N’Djosse, 46, still has no idea where her son, Laurys N’Djosse, is and says the prison blunder has meant she’s “lost all hope”.





Claire, who lives in France, has not seen her son for almost two years after he was abducted by his father, Ifedayo Adeyeye.

The kidnapping took place in France on July 27, 2024 during Laurys’ first overnight stay with his father, where it’s believed he was taken to Nigeria via the UK.

Adeyeye, 58, was jailed for six months for the offence and given an additional 12-month sentence after failing to return Laurys – who is believed to still be in Nigeria – to his mother.

But officials fear he has fled the country after being released before he could start his renewed sentence at HMP Pentonville in North London.

Adeyeye was let out on April 21, but the 12-month warrant was not flagged up – despite being received at 6pm the day before.

Authorities think Adeyeye, a dual British-Nigerian national, may have travelled to Spain in the three days it took prison staff to notify police.



Police are continuing to search for Adeyeye, with the Ministry of Justice saying that it understood the distress the mistaken release had caused.

Claire told Press Association that she was “lost” without her son and that her “life stopped” when Laurys was abducted, leaving her feeling that she was “going to die”.

She continued that Adeyeye’s imprisonment had given her a “glimmer of hope” that Laurys would be returned, but that his release meant “my life stopped again”.

She said: “It’s my child who’s my hope. My life has stopped; I can’t do anything if I don’t have my child. My child is my reason to live.

“Although it was difficult, I told myself, ‘I’m going to live in hope. Now that [Adeyeye] is in the justice system’s hands, whatever happens, I will have my child’. I tried to have the strength.”



“Now that Adeyeye is gone again, I have lost all hope of seeing my child again. I am upset. I don’t know how I’m going to keep going.”

Previously, a Nigerian court had given parental responsibility for Laurys to two people, believed to be Adeyeye’s relatives, without Claire’s consent.

But in a legal first, Mr Justice Hayden ruled that the UK High Court had the power to order that Adeyeye return Laurys to his mother, even though the boy did not live in the UK.

Mr Justice Hayden, who handed Adeyeye the additional year-long sentence and described the lag as a “dangerous threat to his son’s physical and emotional welfare”.

He also called the abduction “an act of cruelty that even this court rarely sees” and added that Adeyeye’s accidental release was a failure by the state, with an “alarming lack of urgency” from prison staff.



Claire says she “felt betrayed” by Pentonville prison where she “believed him to be the most secure” and called for an investigation into Adeyeye’s release, adding she wanted “justice for this injustice”.

She added: “The UK Government must see that it is not OK. I am a victim, I am unfortunately a victim, and it’s very serious.”

Claire believes that Laurys was being “manipulated like a puppet” and urged anyone with information related to Adeyeye’s whereabouts, including his family, to come forward.

She said: “My child wants to come back to see his mum. My child does not deserve all this. Why is my child being punished?”

“I am a lost mum. Without my child, I don’t have a life. I want to find my child.



“I beg you to hear my screams, I beg you, those who are already parents, those who aren’t parents yet, I beg you.”

Data published by the MoJ last month showed that 179 inmates were wrongly released between April 2025 and March 2026.

It is understood that a review into Adeyeye’s release is ongoing, with a spokesperson for the department stating that it had accepted 33 recommendations from an independent review into accidental releases across the prison system.

They said: “We completely understand the distress that this release in error has caused Claire N’Djosse, and our thoughts remain with her and her family.

“We are urgently working with the police to recapture this individual.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The Government inherited a prison system in crisis after years of underinvestment, which has resulted in unacceptable rises in releases in error.

“That’s why we’re investing up to £82 million to digitise outdated paper-based systems, roll out biometrics and strengthen checks so we can better protect the public.”

News.title: Moment 15kg sofa misses shoppers by INCHES after idiot yob, 15, lobs it off Westfield balcony in new footage
News.content:
THIS is the moment a 15kg sofa misses shoppers by mere inches after a 15-year-old chucked it off a shopping centre balcony.

New CCTV shows the teenager throwing furniture inside Westfield in Stratford, London, on March 1 last year – and how close it came to hitting shoppers.





The teen was with a mate at the time and they were both arrested soon after. Neither can be named for legal reasons.

His pal, 16, filmed as the teenager lobbed the massive seat from 50ft up.

The video went viral on social media, with a video captioned “no way bro almost killed someone”.

The pair were prosecuted and now new footage has emerged – showing just how close they came to hitting unsuspecting shoppers.

Video shows a group of three, who had just walked past the spot where the chair landed, turning around in shock after it crashed to the ground.

Other shoppers, who witnessed the scene, can be seen jumping and freezing in fear after it landed – before walking in a different direction.



Surveillance video from the shopping centre’s second floor also shows the moment the teenager picked up the seat and threw it from the balcony before running away.

Stratford Magistrates’ Court heard three weeks before the sofa incident, he was caught chucking pebbles and stones off the balcony at Westfield.

The 16-year-old claimed that he and his friend regularly threw objects off bridges and trains as “pranks”.



He told officers it was “not that deep” and the worst outcome was someone needing “hospital treatment”.

The 15-year-old avoided jail after he admitted criminal damage of the £500 chair.

The boy who filmed it also pleaded guilty to recklessly causing a public nuisance.

He was handed a referral order that includes a three-month curfew and must attend victim awareness intervention.

Sentencing, the judge said: “It is an absolute miracle that no one was harmed.



“It will be obvious to anyone that people escaped some form of personal injury.

“There is no doubt in my mind that this could have caused much higher harm.

“You could have filmed someone being killed that day. More than one person, in fact.”

News.title: Inside the scam gangs taking UK students ‘hostage’ in sick blackmail plot to fleece families out of thousands of pounds
News.content:
WITH bloodied bandages wrapped around his head, the 19-year-old pleads for money from his mum and tells her: “If you refuse, they will cut off my fingers.”

The chilling footage was every parent’s worst nightmare – the university student, who had been missing for ten days, revealed “my whole body is in pain” and “I’m very scared” following a brutal beating at a warehouse. But not all was as it seemed.



The video, showing Xiaoqiang Yu, 19, was fake – part of an elaborate scam targeting the wealthy families of Chinese students enrolled at universities here in the UK.

Cops have called it a “worldwide exploitation” strategy that is rapidly expanding here after success overseas – including in Australia, where online crooks nabbed £2.7million in just five months.

Xiaoqiang and countless other victims are being tricked by fraudsters into believing they have committed a crime or violated their student visa conditions, meaning they could get deported immediately.



During phone calls, they are passed between con artists posing as UK Visas and Immigration officials, Chinese police and prosecutors, who say they can remain in the UK while investigations continue, if they pay sizeable sums.

Their manipulative scam sees some victims forced to send their whereabouts every two hours, uninstall social media apps to cut them off from caregivers and screenshot all of their messages. And sometimes it takes an even darker turn.

Some, like Xiaoqiang, are so “brainwashed” and scared that they are convinced to carry out “virtual kidnappings” of themselves, where they fake injuries and record videos begging their parents for money – one female Southampton student claimed tricksters fleeced her family out of £250,000.

In 2024, Edinburgh University student Xiaoqiang was coerced into travelling 140miles to a Durham hotel to hide away and film his pleas, alongside another student, who was forced to pose as the kidnapper after falling victim to a similar scam.

The case, which has sparked warnings to Chinese students across the UK, features as part of the new documentary series Reported Missing, which is available to stream on iPlayer on BBC One.



Detective Sgt Andy Denhem, of Durham CID, said: “It’s a very unusual case, but it just shows we are in the world with digital tech, that we can have somebody on the other side of the world controlling the actions of people in England and Scotland to obtain large amounts of money.

“I am aware of Chinese students being victims of scams. They are miles away from friends and family and are vulnerable.

“They are contacted by third parties from China, threats are made, such as the threat of being arrested and deported, which would not only affect them but also the pride of the family. This can cause them a lot of fear.”

Police were first alerted to the case when Xiaoqiang was reported missing by his family, who live 5,000 miles away in China, after they had been unable to contact him for five days.

When officers discovered he had been asking for “unusually large sums of money”, his case was elevated to ‘high risk’ and the force tracked his phone to a hotel in Durham.



Answering the door, Xiaoqiang appeared to be in good health and claimed he was trying to escape his “controlling” mother. Due to being an adult, the police closed the case and did not need to inform his family.

But 10 days later, his mum – who did not wish to be named – was terrified after receiving a chilling video clip of her son crying, with apparent bloody wounds, asking for money to ensure his safe release.

Sobbing in the clips, Xiaoqiang says: “Dad, Mum, I’m begging you.



“They took me to a warehouse. They beat me up. Mamma, my head hurts now, my whole body is in pain, I’m very scared, Mum. If you refuse, they will cut off my fingers.”

But the mum, who had complied with previous demands for money, was suspicious and became convinced her son was “under duress” and got back in touch with officers.

Edinburgh Chief Inspector Mark Hamilton, who led the case, told The Sun: “She was absolutely worried out of her mind.”

Cops were able to trace Xiaoqiang’s phone back to the same Durham hotel – but far from being kidnapped, CCTV cameras showed him booking himself in at reception.

Unknown to officers then, his stay in the hotel was the demand of scammers.



They also traced a second victim, who had checked into the same hotel room. He had been instructed to pose as a kidnapper and monitor Xiaoqiang after being blackmailed by the same scammers.

When police arrived at the hotel, Xiaoqiang had vanished and was later found by officers wandering around Durham city centre in a panicked state.

The second man initially denied knowing Xiaoqiang due to fearing what his scammers would do. Eventually, he revealed his involvement in the plot after being probed by police multiple times.

At the Durham police station, officers explained to Xiaoqiang that the ‘officials’ issuing demands and threatening him with deportation if he didn’t send money were actually con artists. He was devastated.

Chief Inspector Hamilton tells us: “What often happens is these individuals are isolated in a different country and continent from their own.



“They are not quite as integrated due to being new here and aren’t as aware of our customs and how we do things, which makes them more vulnerable.

“So if they receive a phone call from someone claiming to be an official, they believe it to be true. They are usually told, ‘You owe us money’ or ‘Pay us this, or something bad will happen to you.'”

The scammers, believed to be based in China, made off with an undisclosed sum said to be “a very large amount of money” by Chief Inspector Hamilton.

The crooks have not been caught due to the family deciding not to press charges.

It’s believed Xiaoqiang was targeted after scammers researched his family, who are wealthy, and knew he would have access to large sums of money.



Chief Inspector Hamilton adds: “The demands are usually quite high, which sometimes suggests awareness of the individual and them likely being able to have access to large amounts of money.

“We have seen various ways of extorting money through different means – including the option, like on this occasion, to make the individual [create the video] themselves.

“It makes their family incredibly worried and concerned, so they are more likely to hand over the money.



“Especially if their family isn’t in the same country, they will go to great lengths to pay the money and do what they think is the right thing.”

Xiaoqiang, who has returned to China after his chilling ordeal, is far from alone in being a victim.

Although Chief Inspector Hamilton couldn’t give figures, he spoke of police being aware of many cases.

In 2023, master’s student Chen, 26, who was enrolled at the University of Southampton, told the BBC she was scammed out of £31,000 by a man posing as a Shanghai police officer in phone calls.

The bogus official said she was suspected of being part of a money laundering scheme and was ordered to send money to the government to check her financial resources.



After Chen sent the funds, the crook vanished. She had to start working two part-time jobs while studying to help her begin to pay off her debt.

She said at the time: “I feel stupid… I don’t know why I got scammed. Last year [was] very hard and full of depression… and I feel very desperate.”

And in 2025, an anonymous Imperial College London student revealed their family was defrauded of £250,000 (2.5million yuan) after fake officials told them they were part of a “high-level international scam case”.

The cruel fraudsters told the victim that if she didn’t comply, she would be “deported immediately”. They donned fake identities of UK immigration workers, police officers and a prosecutors as part of the plot.

They supplied her with official-looking documents, the names of real cops ‘involved in the case’ and their badge numbers, and spoke to her on video calls and using phone numbers from Shanghai’s Public Security Bureau.



As part of the elaborate plot, they demanded she remain on Skype at all times with screen-sharing enabled in a bid to prevent her from speaking to family or friends or raise concerns.

They also demanded she send a “safety report” every two hours – including her name, location, time and current activities.

She was also forced to send screenshots of all websites she visited and messages she had received, and uninstall social media apps.

During one call, the phoney prosecutor told her a victim of ‘her scam’ had taken his own life, according to Imperial’s student publication Felix, which first reported the case.



The scammer gave her two options: return to China to be arrested on arrival and lose out on her education, or pay £250,000 bail to remain in the UK while their investigation continued.

They claimed the money, which the student obtained through lying to her parents about needing funds for an “urgent educational purpose”, would be returned after the case concluded. After it was sent, they vanished.

There are more than 143,200 Chinese students enrolled in courses in the UK – and, while no exact figures on this type of crime are known, it’s clear authorities fear many could be at risk of this “worldwide exploitation” strategy by scammers.

Police forces and universities in Bournemouth, Cornwall, Devon, Edinburgh, Lancashire, Liverpool, London, Sheffield and the West Midlands have all put out warnings online to Chinese students detailing the variety of cons targeting them.



And it’s not just affecting those studying in the UK. In Australia, more than £2.7million was extorted from Chinese students via scams in just five months back in 2025.

From January to June that year, a total of 680 scams were reported to authorities, and 16 victims came forward. The most occurred in May when eight people were defrauded of funds.

Despite tricksters having just a 5.5 per cent success rate, they managed to fleece an average of £73,000 per student, who were predominantly aged 18 to 24.

In the case of Xiaoqiang, no arrests or further legal action were taken due to his family deciding to “draw a line under it” and not press charges. Police, due to a lack of evidence, were not able to pursue it themselves.

Chief Inspector Hamilton said: “It’s frustrating not to see the case to the full conclusion, but we achieved our ultimate aim of finding Xiaoqiang safe.”



He urges individuals in a similar situation “don’t pay” and to contact the police. For those who have been scammed, there are agreements in place to help them to get their money back.

Ch Insp Hamilton adds: “He adds: “If you receive a call and think it’s suspicious please do report it.

“It’s highly unlikely you will be contacted by any kind of official demanding large amounts of money. That’s not going to be the case.

“If you’re being targeted, my advice is don’t pay, think about it carefully and speak to someone officially.

“We treat people with the utmost respect and are sensitive about how we inquire and consider their needs at all times.



“Ultimately, we want to catch these people and stop these crimes from happening again.”

News.title: Heartbreaking new details revealed at inquest after three sisters drowned in sea off Brighton in triple family tragedy
News.content:
THREE sisters who drowned in Brighton were identified by their heartbroken dad following the triple tragedy, an inquest heard.

Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, were tragically pulled from the water on May 13.





It is feared the women were “suddenly dragged into danger after misjudging the shingle shelf” close to the water’s edge.

The triple tragedy came 16 years after their mum Janice, 43, was also found drowned after disappearing in Birmingham.

An inquest heard today how Rebecca’s body washed up on the shore while Christina and Jane were found in the water by the RNLI.

All three siblings were formally identified by their heartbroken dad, the court was told.



The provisional cause of death for the women is yet to be ascertained.

Senior coroner Penelope Schofield confirmed police believe there is no third party involvement in the sisters’ deaths.



She added: “I hope this will stop the social media speculation around the circumstances of their deaths.”

It was heard the sisters lived at the same address in Greenford, West London, and their occupations were unknown.

The coroner also offered her condolences to dad Joseph, who watched the proceedings via videolink.

She said the loss of his daughters must be “unbearable” and adjourned the inquest until October 8.

A frantic search was launched at 5.45am after reports of a person in the water near Brighton.



Emergency services were called to the beach near Black Rock car park off Madeira Drive.

Police later confirmed three women had been pulled from the water.

Officers are probing a number of lines of enquiry with the investigation ongoing.

Sussex Police said there is currently no evidence to suggest third-party involvement or criminality.

The sisters’ dad Joseph said “no words can truly describe the pain” of losing his family after the triple tragedy.



He also described the girls as his “joy and strength” in a moving tribute after they died.

Joseph added: “The tragedy of losing all three of you has left an emptiness that words cannot heal.”

“Today, with a heart full of sorrow and love, I pay tribute to my beloved daughters — Jane, Christina, and Becky — whose lives ended so tragically far too soon.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

His wife Genevieve Barnaby described them as “the most beautiful girls [who] didn’t give us no trouble”.

She posted a tribute to her stepchildren, saying: “Our hearts are broken. The pain is indescribable.”

News.title: Victim 'scared to death' of alleged 'killer who forced him to hand over benefits'
News.content:
Victim 'scared to death' of alleged 'killer who forced him to hand over benefits'

Graham Cox, 37, allegedly "changed" after his encounter with murder-accused Ashley Crowder, 36, as the court heard the defendant denied murder and an alternative charge of manslaughter

View 2 Images Graham Cox was allegedly held hostage by Ashley Crowder (Image: MEN Media)

A murder victim was "scared to death" of an alleged killer who forced him to hand over benefits, a court heard.

‌



Ashley Crowder, 36, denied murdering Graham Cox after the 37-year-old was found dead at the defendant's Bolton flat in March 2024. Bolton Crown Court heard that weeks earlier, Mr Cox attended a support centre alleging he'd been held hostage by Crowder at his flat for the past two weeks and was attacked by him.

‌



Mr Cox, the court heard said he was been able to escape from the flat through a window, before arriving at the UCAN centre in Farnworth, where he regularly attended, to seek help. He claimed Crowder forced him to hand over his benefits money, the Crown told the trial.

‌



View 2 Images Crowder denies murdering Cox (Image: MEN Media)

Crowder, of Barton Walk, Farnworth, denied murder and an alternative charge of manslaughter. He also denied assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and four counts of theft, Manchester Evening News reports.

A video interview with police played at court on Thursday showed Mr Cox's former friend John Mahon saying that after the deceased came out of hospital, he was "petrified of Ashley." He continued: "Before he went into hospital, he could handle himself, after he came out, Ashley changed.

‌



"He [Mr Crowder] kept bragging about chopping his leg. He would belittle him, and used to call him names." He went on to describe one incident in which he said Mr Cox came out from the toilet at Crowder's flat with his trousers not fully pulled up, before he went to sit on the sofa.

Mr Mahon told the jury: "He [Mr Crowder] was screaming at Graham, saying 'what you doing? You're [sitting] your a**e on my couch.'

Graham was saying 'I'm sorry, I'm sorry'. He was scared to death." He told the court Mr Crowder kicked Mr Cox in the chest and "kicked him to the floor."

‌



Mr Mahon claimed he witnessed Mr Cox being scared of Crowder "loads" and that he had seen the defendant "slap Mr Cox to his head behind closed doors." He claimed to have previously been friends with Crowder and Mr Cox and accepted they would take drugs together either at Crowder's flat or another friend's home.

It was put to him by barrister Richard Pratt KC, defending, that he had "turned against" Crowder when he was spoken to by the police about the incident.

Mr Mahon said: "When I spoke to the police, I said he was a horrible, twisted guy. Sick." In re-examination by junior prosecutor Rachel Shenton, he said: "It trauma'd [sic] me, him dying."

Article continues below

The trial continues.

News.content:
A fire broke out on an Amtrak train on track 11 of Manhattan's West Side Yard, causing services to be suspended from New York's Penn Station

A fire broke out on an Amtrak work train on a track in Manhattan's West Side rail yard, causing major disruption at New York's Penn Station - the busiest rail hub in the western hemisphere.

Authorities say five people, believed to be railway employees, were injured and treated for smoke inhalation. Two of these injuries are believed to be serious, ABC7 reports.

News.title: 35p drug taken by millions could increase heart attack risk
News.content:
35p drug taken by millions could increase heart attack risk

Millions of people keep this cheap painkiller in cupboards and handbags without knowing a hidden health risk

View 3 Images Ibuprofen can cost as little as 35p (Image: Iuliia Bondar)

Many people rely on a cheap everyday painkiller to get through headaches, back pain and aches and pains without giving it a second thought. But health experts warn the common medicine may come with a little-known risk that can become more serious the more frequently it is taken.

‌



The drug, which can cost as little as 35p in supermarkets and pharmacies across the country, is used by millions across the UK every year. While many people take it occasionally without issue, research suggests regular or high-dose use could raise the risk of serious heart problems.

‌



Ibuprofen belongs to a group of medicines known as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which are commonly used to reduce pain, inflammation and fever. According to the NHS, side effects can include nausea, indigestion and headaches, though more serious complications can occur in some people.

‌



The NHS warns people should seek urgent medical help if they experience symptoms including chest tightness, trouble breathing or signs of a heart attack after taking ibuprofen. Guidance also states the medicine may not be suitable for people who have high blood pressure, coronary heart disease, heart failure or circulation problems.

View 3 Images Ibuprofen is one of the most popular painkillers in the UK (Image: Peter Dazeley)

According to research highlighted by Harvard Health, taking certain NSAIDs daily — including ibuprofen — was linked to a 20 to 50 per cent higher risk of heart attack compared to people not taking the drugs. The report, published in The BMJ, found the risk could begin increasing within the first week of use, particularly at higher doses.

‌



Harvard Health said the “most harmful doses” appeared to be more than 1,200mg of ibuprofen per day. Experts added that while the overall risk for healthy people remains relatively small, it becomes more concerning in older adults and those with existing cardiovascular conditions.

Another Harvard Health report explained that all non-aspirin NSAIDs appear to carry some degree of heart risk. It added that the longer the drugs are taken and the higher the dosage, the greater the potential danger becomes.

The NHS advises adults should not take more than 1,200mg of ibuprofen a day without speaking to a doctor. It also recommends taking the lowest dose needed for the shortest possible amount of time.

‌



View 3 Images Ibuprofen can lead to chest tightness (Image: Getty Images)

According to the Mayo Clinic, the increased risk of heart attack and stroke affects both people with heart disease and those without it. However, specialists say the risk is greater in people who already have underlying cardiovascular problems.

Harvard Health has also pointed to evidence suggesting NSAIDs may increase blood pressure and cause fluid retention, which can place extra strain on the cardiovascular system. Researchers say this may partly explain why long-term or high-dose use has been associated with heart attacks and strokes.

Article continues below

Health professionals stress people should not suddenly stop prescribed medication without medical advice. Anyone worried about side effects or needing regular pain relief is advised to speak with a GP or pharmacist about the safest treatment options available.

News.title: £200k Aston Martin wrecked as windows smashed and 'CHEATER' spray painted on car at luxury London golf club
News.content:
£200k Aston Martin wrecked as windows smashed and 'CHEATER' spray painted on car at luxury London golf club

A witness captured a mystery man walking away after the vehicle had its windows, lights and roof smashed with a hammer and the word 'cheater' written across the bonnet

View 3 Images A mystery man is believed to have damaged the vehicle (Image: TeddingtonTown.co.uk / SWNS)

A luxury car worth almost £200k was wrecked by a furious mystery man in a golf club car park.

‌



The windows of the Aston Martin were smashed by a mystery man as ‘CHEATER’ was spray-painted on the bonnet. The man, seen wearing a baseball cap, was spotted destroying the 2015 Vanquish at Hampton Court Palace Golf Club in South West London on Monday.

‌



The details of the attack is yet to be confirmed, as the Metropolitan Police investigate the damage, which appears to be a result of a cheating scandal. Video footage taken in the aftermath of the incident showed a man walking away from the vehicle, before revealing the extent of the damage.

‌



View 3 Images The Metropolitan Police said it was investigating the incident. (Image: TeddingtonTown.co.uk / SWNS)

A witness who took video footage described seeing the masked man take out a hammer from his rucksack before he wrecked the vehicle, smashing the windows, lights and tearing the roof open. The rear-wheel drive car personalised with the numberplate ‘BD55 BOB’ was sprayed with what appeared to be the word ‘CHEATER’ in white across the bonnet.

‌



The high-end car, which retails for as much as £192,000 when new, is capable of reaching a top speed of 201 mph and accelerating from 0 to 52 mph in just 3.6 seconds. But after the damage, the car was declared a 'write-off'.

View 3 Images Footage captured the mystery man (Image: TeddingtonTown.co.uk / SWNS)

The Metropolitan Police said it was investigating the incident. The force spoke to the witness as well as the owner of the car, who had been walking his dogs at the time.

Article continues below

The force said: "Police were called at around 14:00hrs on Monday, 25 May to reports of criminal damage to a vehicle at a sports club in Dillon Close, Molesey. Officers attended and searched the area, but were unable to locate the suspect. No arrests have been made, and enquiries continue."

Anyone with information is asked to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 4251/25MAY or Crimestoppers, anonymously, on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Island loved by Brits bans new holiday lets in overtourism crackdown
News.content:
Island loved by Brits bans new holiday lets in overtourism crackdown

The Spanish destination has banned all new holiday rental properties — including houses and villas — as local authorities move to protect struggling residents from being pushed out of their own neighbourhoods

View 2 Images Local politicians are moving ahead with plans to limit Airbnb supply (Image: Jam Press/Helen Dalling)

A beloved holiday destination popular with British tourists is cracking down on new holiday rental properties, after they were found to be forcing local residents out of their own communities.

‌



Local politicians in Palma de Majorca are poised to bring in the measure to boost housing availability for hard-pressed residents. New licensed apartment holiday lets have already been prohibited there for several years, and now local politicians are moving forward with a ban on houses and villas.

‌



Local councillor Óscar Fidalgo insisted the move was one that simply had to be made. He described it as proportionate and fair, adding that it should have been implemented sooner in order to protect those living on the island from spiking property prices.

‌



He was openly critical of holiday rentals growing 'like never before', and warned that they were causing integration issues between tourists and locals.

View 2 Images Majorca has been struggling with housing for years (Image: Jam Press)

Popular UK holiday spot is closing to tourists one day a week READ MORE :

Brit holidaymakers stuck on Greek island thanks to little-known rule READ MORE :

According to Majorca Daily Bulletin, Fidalgo said: "The expansion of tourist accommodation reduces the available residential supply and makes it harder to access housing. The current model presents problems of legal certainty and complicates inspections, which allows for fraud. More inspection capacity is needed.

‌



"There are also urban sustainability reasons. It affects neighbourhood coexistence. We must protect neighbourhoods and prevent the displacement of residents."

A town hall technical report concluded that the Spanish holiday hotspot is unsuitable for the opening of new holiday rental properties.

In April this year, more than 8,000 illegal Airbnb listings in Majorca were removed from the website, totaling a withdrawal of more than 40,000 illegal tourist beds.

‌



The move was part of a coordinated effort between Airbnb and the Spanish authorities to reduce the number of active rental properties.

The fines for running an unlicensed holiday let in Palma de Majorca are steep. Landlords face fines of up to €40,000 (£34,700) and the government has employed a group of inspectors to ensure compliance. There is also an online reporting system for the public to report suspected rule-breakers to the authorities.

Nearly a third of tourists visiting Spain opt to stay in short-term rentals. The number of homes listed for holiday rentals in May dropped 6% from the previous summer to 1.43 million, after regulations were tightened to ease the housing crisis, data from the National Statistics Institute showed.

Article continues below

According to campaign group Affordable Majorca, since 2013, rents in Palma have increased by a whopping 40%.

Approximately 2.3 to 3.6 million British tourists visit Mallorca each year. The UK consistently ranks as the second-largest source of international visitors to the island, making up about 20% to 26% of all tourist traffic, trailing just behind Germany, according to Road Genius.

The decision in Palma de Majorca comes as another holiday island has also cracked down on beach regulations, banning nearly 700 loungers. Authorities imposed the ban on Formentera in the Balearics, effective immediately until 2029. A further 339 parasols have also been ordered to be removed from beaches.

News.title: 'I'm an Independent Financial Adviser and new HMRC double tax is coming'
News.content:
'I'm an Independent Financial Adviser and new HMRC double tax is coming'

People have until April 6, 2027, to take action

View 3 Images Samuel Mather-Holgate (Image: Newspage)

An expert has warned of a double tax trap coming next year that leaves "people shocked when they see the maths written down".

‌



Millions of families could face a major pension tax shock from April 2027, with experts warning that inherited pension wealth may end up being hit by both inheritance tax and income tax at the same time. For years, pensions have been viewed as one of the most tax-efficient ways to pass wealth down to the next generation because unused pension pots generally sat outside a person’s estate for inheritance tax purposes.

‌



But that is set to change from April 6, 2027, when most unused pension funds and pension death benefits will be brought into scope for inheritance tax by HMRC. Financial advisers say many families still do not fully appreciate how severe the combined tax impact could become.

‌



View 3 Images It could cause unexpected problems at a difficult time (Image: clubfoto via Getty Images)

Samuel Mather-Holgate, managing director and Independent Financial Adviser at Swindon-based Mather and Murray Financial, said some beneficiaries could ultimately lose more than two-thirds of inherited pension wealth once both taxes were applied.

He added: “A lot of people still assume pensions are safely outside inheritance tax, but from April 2027 that assumption could become dangerously outdated. The real problem is that families may not just face inheritance tax. In some cases, beneficiaries could then pay income tax on top when they draw money from the inherited pension.”

‌



That is where the so-called “67% tax trap” comes from. If a pension fund is first hit by 40% inheritance tax, only 60% of the original pot remains. If the beneficiary then pays income tax at 45% on withdrawals from that remaining amount, the combined effect means 67% of the original pension wealth disappears to tax overall.

In some cases, the tax hit could become even more severe. Beneficiaries paying Scotland’s top 48% income tax rate could lose almost 69% overall, while those caught in the personal allowance taper zone could effectively face a combined tax hit of up to 76% on part of the inherited pension.

Mr Mather-Holgate said: “People are understandably shocked when they see the maths written down properly. This is not some theoretical loophole or gimmick. It is simply two separate tax systems potentially colliding with one another.”

‌



He warned that the changes could fundamentally alter traditional retirement and inheritance planning strategies. For many years, advisers often encouraged retirees to spend other assets first while leaving pensions untouched for as long as possible because of their favourable inheritance treatment. But that logic may now need revisiting.

View 3 Images The HMRC change begins next tax year (Image: Yau Ming Low via Getty Images)

Mr Mather-Holgate said: “This could completely change the old ‘spend your ISA first and preserve your pension’ strategy. That does not mean everybody should suddenly empty their pension, but it does mean families need to review whether their current plans still make sense under the new rules.”

Article continues below

He said many people also underestimate how important beneficiary planning could become: “A pension left to one beneficiary could create a very different tax outcome compared to leaving it to somebody else in a lower tax bracket. Beneficiary nominations are no longer just admin paperwork. They are becoming a key part of tax planning.”

Despite the looming changes, Mr Mather-Holgate stressed there were still opportunities to reduce the eventual damage through proper financial planning, gifting strategies and reviewing how pensions fit into wider estate plans. But he warned that many families were leaving things late.

He added: “The worst time to discover a double-tax problem is after somebody has died. From now until April 2027, people have a window to review their arrangements properly before these rules potentially start biting.”

News.title: The burning questions Brits wish they could ask their pets – as podcast launches
News.content:
The burning questions Brits wish they could ask their pets – as podcast launches

A survey of 2,000 pet owners has uncovered the top 25 questions dog and cat owners wish they could ask their furry friends - from 'are you happy?' to 'do you ever judge me?'

James Hoyles explains pet ownership habits in Q&A

'Are you happy?', 'Do you like me?' and 'Do you talk about me to other animals?' feature amongst the top 25 questions pet owners wish they could ask their beloved companions.

‌



A survey of 2,000 cat and dog owners discovered that 54% frequently wish they could have a conversation with their four-legged friends to gain a deeper understanding of their thoughts and feelings.

‌



Roughly one in 10 cat owners have pondered what their pet might be scheming, while 36% suspect their feline may actually be able to read their mind.

‌



Meanwhile, one in five dog owners are keen to know whether their pet could be autistic. Others revealed they'd love to discover whether their animals are passing judgement on them – or whether they experience jealousy.

View 2 Images Actor James Hoyles also has plenty of questions for his dog Trevor (Image: PinPep)

This follows pet insurer Petgevity, which commissioned the study, launching its first ever podcast this week, focusing on neurodiversity in pets. Doctor Who actor James Hoyles and his four-legged companion Trevor the Iggy have joined forces with the insurer for the project.

‌



The actor and content creator said: "Having a pet means you never stop learning, especially when you realise just how complex they can be.

"No pet is the same – every animal is different and will have different needs, and it is completely normal to have questions you never expected to ask."

The study also found that 88% of owners are confident they understand their pet, with 41% claiming their pet understands them better than any other human.

‌



Four in ten frequently find themselves talking to their pet as if they were human, routinely seeking their counsel on major life decisions, such as a new job or a relationship breakup, despite knowing they won't get a response.

View 2 Images Many owners believe their pets have human-like qualities (Image: PinPep)

Many have also pictured their pet possessing human characteristics, such as a preferred type of food (43%), a distinctive sense of humour (32%), and caring about their appearance (21%).

‌



However, some would like to probe deeper, with pressing questions centred on their pet-owner bond, such as 'what's your favourite thing we do together?' (34%) and 'do you wish I did anything differently?' (33%)

Kerry Willecome, pet insurance expert at Petgevity, added: "They aren't just pets but friends and members of our family.

"We develop deep meaningful connections with our pets which is why it's always worth seeking trusted advice when something doesn't seem quite right

Article continues below

"And the fact owners always have questions about their furry friends just goes to show how much they want to understand their pets and make them happy."

News.title: Are 'heat spikes' becoming more common?
News.content:
With temperatures hitting a record breaking 35.1C this week, it has been an exceptional May heatwave.

In its build up we saw temperatures increase rapidly - by up to 10C in just two days in some locations.

Historically, it would have been more common to see a gradual increase of a degree or two each day.

The rapid onset from an average to high, even extreme, temperature - or a "heat spike" - is something I and fellow meteorologists have noticed happening more often.

Ed Hawkins, professor of climate science at the University of Reading, told the BBC that "Today's heat events are emerging earlier, intensifying faster and occurring across a much warmer background climate".

While according to Dr SÃ©golÃ¨ne Berthou from the Met Office, "We can't explicitly say that extreme heat temperatures spike faster now than they did in the past," experts are beginning to piece together a number of other factors that could provide an explanation.
